conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Moore, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and to check on how you’re feeling emotionally.  

Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a brief, 10-question screen that asks about mood, anxiety, and thoughts you may have had over the past seven days. Your answers are confidential, and there are no right or wrong responses; we simply want to understand how you’re coping so we can offer the best support.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no check-boxes on your end—and we’ll take it at your pace. Whenever you’re ready, here’s the first one:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

*shifts slightly in the chair, eyes downcast*

Honestly... I can't remember the last time I really laughed. My sister came over yesterday and was telling me about something funny that happened at her work, and I just... couldn't. I managed a little smile because I didn't want to seem rude, but it felt like such an effort. Everything just feels so heavy lately, like I have to fake finding things amusing when inside I just feel... empty, I guess.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

No… not really. I mean, I *try*—like when my partner makes a joke—but the laughter just doesn’t come. I’ll smile so he doesn’t worry, but it feels forced. Even when I see other moms giggling with their babies on social media, I wonder, “Why can’t I feel that light?” Everything feels muted, like I’m watching life through a fogged window.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*wrings hands in lap*

I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park, even just a quiet shower. Now… nothing really feels worth looking forward to. My mom offered to watch the baby so I could get a haircut next week, and I said “sure,” but inside I felt nothing. No spark. I keep thinking, “What’s the point? I’ll still come home to the same pile of laundry, the same crying, the same me who can’t seem to get it right.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, eyes filling with tears*

All the time. Yesterday he wouldn’t settle for his nap—just cried and cried—and I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong. Maybe I’m not feeding him right, or I’m holding him wrong, or I waited too long to put him down. My partner came home and got him to sleep in five minutes, and I just sat there feeling like… like I’m failing at the one thing I’m supposed to be made for. I know rationally babies cry, but my head keeps saying, “A good mom would know how to fix it.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*fidgets with the edge of the baby-blanket in my lap*

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing—even though she’s right there, eyes open, perfectly fine. Or I’ll lie down at night and picture her crib suddenly collapsing, or the stroller rolling into the street. I know it’s unlikely, but I can’t shake the what-ifs. Sometimes I have to get up three or four times to check on her, and even after that I still feel tense, like I’m waiting for something bad to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*clenches and unclenches hands, voice shaky*

A few times this week, yeah. It’s like a wave hits me out of nowhere—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s changed. Last night the baby was asleep, the house was quiet, and suddenly I felt like the walls were closing in. I had to turn on all the lights and pace the hallway just to feel like I could still breathe. It passes after a while, but in those moments I feel completely out of control.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods slowly, exhaling*

Yes… most days. It feels like the minute I finish one feeding, the next is already due, the laundry’s piled higher, and I haven’t eaten anything real since breakfast yesterday. I start a task and get interrupted by crying, then completely forget what I was doing. By evening I’m staring at the mess, thinking, “I’ll never catch up.” I keep telling myself other moms manage, so why can’t I stay on top of simple things like folding a basket of onesies or replying to a text.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*pulls cardigan tighter around shoulders*

Yeah… pretty much every night this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—going over everything I think I did wrong, worrying about the next feed, replaying every cry. I finally drift off, then jolt awake sure I heard her when she’s actually still asleep. Once I’m up it’s impossible to settle again; I just stare at the ceiling feeling this heavy sadness, watching the hours tick by until she needs me.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice drops to almost a whisper*

Most of the day, every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud parked over me. I’ll be holding the baby, doing everything I’m “supposed” to do, but inside I just feel hollow and weepy. Sometimes I catch myself staring out the window, tears rolling down without me even noticing at first. I keep thinking, “I should be grateful—he’s healthy, we’re safe,” but the sadness just sits there, heavy on my chest.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, eyes watering again*

Yeah… it’s happened three, maybe four times this week. Sometimes it’s triggered by something small—like spilling a bottle I just pumped—but other times it’s nothing I can name. I’ll just be rocking her and the tears start. I try to stay quiet so she doesn’t see, but once I start I can’t stop for a while. It leaves me feeling even more exhausted, like I’ve got no tears left but they keep coming anyway.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No… never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and hopeless, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. My baby needs me, and no matter how low I feel, I couldn’t leave her.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**

**Patient-reported symptoms:**
- Persistent low mood, “hollow,” tearful most days
- Marked anhedonia (no pleasure in social, self-care, or infant activities)
- Daily excessive guilt/self-blame regarding parenting adequacy
- Frequent, unprovoked anxiety and catastrophic worries about infant safety
- Multiple sudden panic episodes (chest tightness, breathlessness, fear of doom)
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to ruminating and hypervigilant checking
- Overwhelmed/“can’t catch up,” low energy, poor concentration
- Crying spells (≥3 this week) with no clear trigger
- No self-harm ideation; protective toward infant

**Patterns/significance:**
- Consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety
- Functional impairment evident (household tasks, self-care, social withdrawal)
- Hypervigilant infant-focused worries and panic symptoms suggest possible postpartum anxiety component
- Absence of suicidal intent (protective factor), but distress and impairment warrant prompt follow-up

**Recommendation (screening only):**
Score indicates high likelihood of postpartum mood/anxiety disorder; refer for comprehensive psychiatric evaluation and consider supports for safety planning and maternal-infant functioning.
